Publications
Why Evaluating the Impact of AI Needs to Start Now
with Oliver House, Miriam Light & Elizabeth Shelmerdine · Nature, 2024 (perspective)
Paper
Does Reason-Giving Affect Political Attitudes?
Forthcoming, British Journal of Political Science, 2024
Paper Abstract
What are the effects of reason-giving on political attitudes? Both political philosophers and political scientists have speculated that defending proposals with reasons may change voters' preferences. However, while models of attitude formation predict that the explicit justification of one's political views may result in attitudes that are more ideologically consistent, less polarized, and more stable, empirical work has not assessed the connection between reason-giving and attitudes. Implementing a survey experiment in which some respondents provide reasons before stating their opinions on six issues in UK politics, I find that reason-giving has very limited effects on the constraint, stability, or polarization of the public's political attitudes.
Citizens' Preferences for Multidimensional Representation
with Chris Wratil & Fabio Wolkenstein · Forthcoming, Perspectives on Politics, 2024
Paper Abstract
How do citizens want to be represented in politics? We investigate citizens' multidimensional preferences regarding six conceptions of representation that figure prominently in political theory but of which some have been overlooked in empirical work. Using original item batteries and a conjoint experiment, we elicit the relative importance of the dimensions and the types of representation people prefer on each. Our results from surveys fielded in the USA, the UK, and Germany show that descriptive representation has limited appeal for citizens at large but is important for historically marginalized groups; citizens do not focus on local politicians when thinking about who represents them; and while citizens strongly value substantive representation, they are largely indifferent as to whether their representatives are responsive to electoral sanctions.
Polarization over the Priority of Political Problems
with Benjamin E. Lauderdale · Forthcoming, American Journal of Political Science, 2024
Paper Abstract
What drives ideological division about political problems? When prioritising which problems are most in need of redress, voters might disagree about the severity of individual outcomes, the prevalence of those problems, or whether such problems are amenable to solution by government action. We field a large survey experiment in the UK and US and develop a new measurement approach which allows us to evaluate how ideological disagreements change when respondents consider the individual badness, social severity, and priority for government action of a set of 41 political problems. We find that large ideological divergences are observed in beliefs about social severity and priority for government action, not individual problem badness, and only in the US.
Liberals and Conservatives Rely on Very Similar Sets of Foundations When Comparing Moral Violations
with Benjamin E. Lauderdale · American Political Science Review, 2024
Paper Abstract
Moral Foundations Theory aims to explain the origins of and variation in human moral reasoning. Applications in political science have revealed differences in the degree to which liberals and conservatives explicitly endorse five core moral foundations. However, differences in self-reported assessments do not imply that citizens with different political orientations respond to concrete scenarios based on different moral intuitions. We introduce a new approach for measuring the implicit importance of the five moral foundations by asking respondents from the UK and the US to compare pairs of vignettes describing violations relevant to each foundation. Our results suggest that, despite prominent claims to the contrary, voters on the left and the right of politics share broadly similar moral intuitions.
Testing Negative: The Non-Consequences of COVID-19 on Mass Ideology
with Timothy Hicks, Alan M. Jacobs, J. Scott Matthews & Tom O'Grady · Forthcoming, Journal of Politics, 2024
Paper Abstract
In response to the COVID-19 pandemic governments implemented large-scale economic and social policies unprecedented in scale and scope outside of wartime. We hypothesise that exposure to the pandemic and these policy responses caused ideological change, including attitudes to the role of government in the economy and redistribution. Using data from the British Election Study Internet Panel and a unique panel survey, we find virtually no evidence that the pandemic affected ideological beliefs about the role of government or economic and social policy attitudes. We conclude that the pandemic was not, and could not have been, a cause of mass ideological change.
Using Automated Text Classification to Explore Uncertainty in NICE Appraisals for Drugs for Rare Diseases
with Lea Weidmann, John Cairns & Orlagh Carroll · International Journal of Technology Assessment in Health Care, 2023
Paper Abstract
This study examined the application of supervised learning models for text classification in NICE appraisals for rare disease treatments in relation to uncertainty. We analysed 94 appraisals published between 2011 and 2023, using Naive Bayes, Lasso, and SVM models to classify paragraphs as either referencing uncertainty in the evidence base or not. The best-performing model achieved 83.6% classification accuracy. Paragraphs classified as referencing uncertainty were significantly more likely to arise in HST appraisals compared to TA appraisals.
Risk and Health Policy Preferences: Evidence from the UK COVID-19 Crisis
with Raluca Pahontu & Timothy Hicks · British Journal of Political Science, 2023
Paper Abstract
We investigate whether individuals subject to larger increases in objective health risk during COVID-19 became more supportive of increased government healthcare spending. Using panel data tracking UK individuals before and after the outbreak, we implement a pre-registered fixed-effect design. While individuals in high-risk occupations were more worried about personal infection risk and had higher death rates, there is no evidence that increased health risks shifted attitudes on government spending on healthcare or broader redistribution.
No Longer Conforming to Stereotypes? Gender, Political Style, and Parliamentary Debate in the UK
with Lotte Hargrave · British Journal of Political Science, 2022
Paper Abstract
Research on political style suggests that women make arguments that are more emotional, empathetic, and positive, while men use language that is more analytical, aggressive, and complex. We argue that pressures for female politicians to conform to stereotypically 'feminine' styles have diminished in recent years. Analysing UK parliamentary debates between 1997 and 2019, we show that female MPs' debating styles have changed substantially over time, as women in parliament have increasingly adopted stylistic traits typically associated with 'masculine' stereotypes of communication.
The Variable Persuasiveness of Political Rhetoric
with Benjamin E. Lauderdale · American Journal of Political Science, 2022
Paper Abstract
Which types of political rhetoric are most persuasive? Politicians make arguments that share common rhetorical elements, including metaphor, ad hominem attacks, appeals to expertise, moral appeals, and many others. We report on a novel experimental design assessing the relative persuasiveness of a large number of arguments across a range of UK political issues. We find modest differences in the average effectiveness of rhetorical elements, but also large variation in the persuasiveness of arguments of the same rhetorical type across issues.
Measuring Attitudes towards Public Spending Using a Multivariate Tax Summary Experiment
with Lucy Barnes & Benjamin E. Lauderdale · American Journal of Political Science, 2021
Paper Abstract
We present a new measurement strategy using UK taxpayer summaries as the baseline for a continuous treatment, multivariate choice experiment. The experiment proposes deficit-neutral bundles of changes in spending and taxation, allowing us to investigate attitudes towards modifications to the existing budget. We find that the UK public favours paying more in tax to finance large spending increases across major budget categories; that spending preferences are multidimensional; and that younger people prefer lower levels of taxation and spending than older people.
Online Activism and Dyadic Representation: Evidence from the UK E-Petition System
Legislative Studies Quarterly, 2020
Paper Abstract
Using new data from an e-petition system in the UK, I show that support for a petition amongst a Member of Parliament's constituents substantially increases the probability that the MP advocates for the petition in parliamentary debate. However, MP responsiveness is conditioned both by party discipline and electoral competition. These findings have important implications for our understanding of dyadic representation in parliamentary systems.
Parliamentary Debate in the UK House of Commons
with Roberta Damiani · The Politics of Legislative Debate, 2020 (book chapter)
Abstract
We describe the institutional setting of parliamentary debate in the UK House of Commons and assess the determinants of participation using data on more than two million speeches from 1979 to 2019. We show that the main determinant of participation is whether an MP holds an institutionally powerful position. The speech-making bonus enjoyed by those in leadership positions has decreased over time, while MPs have increasingly employed constituency-oriented language in their parliamentary speeches over the past 40 years.
Model-Based Pre-Election Polling for National and Sub-National Outcomes in the US and UK
with Benjamin E. Lauderdale, Delia Bailey & Douglas Rivers · International Journal of Forecasting, 2020
Paper Abstract
We describe a strategy for applying multilevel regression and post-stratification (MRP) methods to pre-election polling. Using contemporaneous polling, census data, and past election results, we construct probabilistic, internally consistent estimates of national vote and sub-national outcomes. We report on three applications: the 2016 UK EU Referendum, the 2016 US Presidential Election, and the 2017 UK General Election.
The Effects of Female Leadership on Women's Voice in Political Debate
British Journal of Political Science, 2019
Paper Abstract
Do female leaders amplify the voices of other women in politics? Examining parliamentary debates in the UK House of Commons, I demonstrate that female ministers substantially increase the participation and influence of other female MPs in relevant debates. Using a new metric of ministerial responsiveness, I show that female ministers are significantly more responsive to the speeches of female backbenchers than are male ministers.
Never Let a Good Crisis Go to Waste: Agenda Setting and Legislative Voting in Response to the EU Crisis
with Benjamin E. Lauderdale · Journal of Politics, 2017
Paper Abstract
When exogenous shocks make status quo policies less attractive, legislators become more tolerant to proposed alternatives further from their ideal. This increases the discretion of agenda-setters, allowing them to pass policy that would have been impossible without a crisis. We argue this dynamic explains changes in European Parliament voting during the financial crisis, with pro-integration actors shifting policy further towards integration than they could have otherwise.
Open/Closed List and Party Choice: Experimental Evidence from the UK
with Andrew C. Eggers, Dominik Hangartner & Simon Hix · British Journal of Political Science, 2016
Paper Abstract
Which parties benefit from open-list proportional representation? We show that a move from closed-list to open-list competition is likely to be more favourable to parties with more internal disagreement on salient issues. Experimental evidence from a hypothetical European Parliament election in the UK demonstrates that using an open-list ballot would shift support from UKIP to Eurosceptic candidates of the Conservative Party, suggesting that open-list ballots could restrict support for single-issue parties.
